analysis.one_liner: Repeals Medicare's drug price negotiation, inflation rebates, and the out-of-pocket drug cost cap.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal Medicare's new drug price negotiation program and out-of-pocket cap never got a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the main prescription drug pricing provisions Congress had just enacted in the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022. It would end Medicare's new program of negotiating drug prices, eliminate rebates on drugs whose prices rise faster than inflation, and remove the new annual cap on what seniors pay out of pocket for prescriptions. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Brand-name drug manufacturers would gain if this bill passed: they would no longer face Medicare-negotiated prices, inflation-based rebates, or the rebate cap on out-of-pocket drug spending that Congress had just enacted in the Inflation Reduction Act, and they could charge prices unbound by those limits. [S2] [S3]

how_it_helps.text: For drug makers, the bill removes the requirement to sell selected drugs to Medicare at prices set through the new negotiation program, restoring full pricing discretion.
For drug makers, it eliminates the inflation rebate, so they could once again raise Medicare drug prices faster than inflation without penalty.

analysis.who_pays: Seniors and people with disabilities on Medicare would bear the cost, through restored unlimited out-of-pocket drug spending and no negotiated prices, and the government would forgo the savings the IRA programs were designed to produce.
analysis.who_pays_short: Seniors on Medicare with drug costs

drawbacks.text: Supporters of repeal argued, as the bill's title suggests, that price negotiation could reduce the financial reward for developing new drugs and slow future innovation.
Repeal would raise costs for seniors: removing the $2,000 annual out-of-pocket cap under the Medicare drug benefit would restore potentially unlimited drug spending for the sickest beneficiaries.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The only beneficiaries of this bill would be brand-name drug manufacturers, and the cost would fall directly on Medicare beneficiaries and the federal budget. The strongest argument in its favor, that price controls may discourage investment in new medicines, is a genuine policy debate, but this bill offered nothing in exchange for taking away the three main new drug affordability protections: it was a straight repeal. Had it passed, seniors with expensive prescriptions would have lost the annual out-of-pocket cap and the inflation rebate protection.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and sat there until the Congress ended, never getting a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 27, 2022 by Sen. Mike Lee with three Republican cosponsors.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where no further action was taken.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 without the bill receiving a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, so nothing was repealed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off, because the Medicare negotiation program, inflation rebates, and the out-of-pocket cap all remain in force instead of being repealed. Medicare beneficiaries are better off relative to what the bill would have done, since their drug price protections stayed intact.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pharmaceutical makers kept their pricing freedom

against.name: Senate Finance Committee leadership (Chair Ron Wyden)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only four sponsors, all Republicans, and died in committee without a vote from either party's full membership.

industries.note: The bill would remove all three of the IRA's main drug pricing constraints, restoring the industry's freedom to set prices, raise them faster than inflation, and rely on Medicare to pay. Its interest in this bill runs directly against the pocketbooks of Medicare beneficiaries.
The Part D out-of-pocket cap and negotiated prices lower what the program pays for prescriptions; repeal would restore higher federal spending on the same drugs.
